title: Process synchronization
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe race conditions, critical sections, and classic semaphore problems to test whether candidates can reason about shared state and concurrency bugs.

phases.goal: Establish that sharing creates synchronization problems, what a race condition is, and what a correct critical-section solution must guarantee.

must_hit.point: Synchronization applies only to cooperative processes that share state; independent processes share no state and their interleaving does not matter.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts independent (no shared state) vs cooperative (share variables, memory, code, or resources) and states sharing is the prerequisite for a sync problem.

must_hit.point: A race condition is when concurrent access to shared data makes the final value depend on timing/order of execution, typically because read–modify–write is not atomic.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gives the definition and ties it to a non-atomic read–modify–write on shared data.

must_hit.point: In the shared-variable race example starting at shared = 5, both processes can read 5 before either writes, so the result is 6 or 4 instead of the expected 5.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks the interleaving: both read 5, then last writer leaves shared at 6 (P1 last) or 4 (P2 last), not 5.

must_hit.point: A critical section is the code that accesses shared resources; entry/exit sections must enforce mutual exclusion, progress (primary), plus bounded waiting and no hardware-speed assumptions (secondary).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the four requirements and marks mutual exclusion and progress as primary.

probes: What is a race condition, and why does sharing writable state make process interleaving matter?
What four requirements must a correct critical-section solution satisfy?

hints.1: Think about what must be true for two processes' interleaving to affect a result.
hints.2: Start from cooperative vs independent, then define race and critical section with mutual exclusion and progress.
hints.3: Race: final shared value depends on uncontrolled order because RMW is not atomic. CS solution needs mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting, and no relative-speed assumptions.

phases.goal: Explain how naive locks fail, how hardware and software solutions enforce mutual exclusion, and how semaphores block instead of busy-wait.

must_hit.point: A plain lock variable fails mutual exclusion because the test (while LOCK == 1) and set (LOCK = 1) are separate non-atomic steps, so two processes can both see LOCK free and enter.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows both processes pass the spin while LOCK is 0, both set LOCK = 1, and both enter the CS.

must_hit.point: test-and-set is an atomic read-then-write-TRUE; spinning until it returns FALSE guarantees mutual exclusion; compare-and-swap is the more general modern form.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes atomic test-and-set entry (spin while true) and unlock by setting lock FALSE, and may mention CAS.

must_hit.point: Strict turn alternation gives mutual exclusion but violates progress: a process that just finished cannot re-enter until the other takes a turn, even if the other is in its remainder and does not want the CS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states ME holds but progress fails under strict alternation, and may mention Peterson's flag[]+turn fix as the correct two-process software answer.

must_hit.point: A semaphore is an integer touched only by atomic down/up (P/V); a blocked process sleeps on a suspended list. Counting semaphores guard resource pools; binary semaphores hold only 0 or 1. A negative counting value equals how many waiters are asleep.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines down/up, sleep vs busy-wait, counting vs binary, and negative value = waiter count.

must_hit.point: With mutex initialized to 1 around down/CS/up, at most one process is in the CS; if initialized to k, up to k processes may be inside simultaneously.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate answers 'at most one' for init 1, and 'up to k' for a counting init of k.

probes: Why does a simple shared LOCK variable fail mutual exclusion?
How does test-and-set differ from a software lock variable, and what do down/up on a semaphore do?

hints.1: Look at whether the check and the update of the lock happen as one step.
hints.2: Contrast non-atomic test-then-set, atomic test-and-set, turn alternation's progress bug, then semaphore sleep lists.
hints.3: LOCK fails because two can both see 0; TAS is atomic so only one sees FALSE; turn violates progress; semaphore down may sleep and negative value counts waiters.

phases.goal: Surface mutex vs spinlock, semaphore vs mutex ownership, and related production concurrency tradeoffs grounded in the lecture.

must_hit.point: A mutex sleeps a blocked waiter (no wasted CPU, but context-switch/wakeup latency of roughly a microsecond or more); a spinlock busy-waits with near-zero acquire latency but burns CPU every spin cycle.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts sleep vs spin and mentions mutex wakeup cost vs spin's burned cycles.

must_hit.point: Spin only when the critical section is shorter than a context switch (rule of thumb: a few microseconds) or when sleeping is impossible (e.g. interrupt handler); otherwise use a mutex. User-space spinlocks are dangerous if the holder is preempted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the short-CS / cannot-sleep rule and the preemption hazard for user-space spinning.

must_hit.point: A semaphore is a signalling device with no owner (any process may up it); a mutex is a lock with ownership (only the locker unlocks). A binary semaphore can act as a mutex, but a mutex cannot provide cross-process signalling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate clearly separates ownership/signalling and states the one-way substitutability.

probes: When would you choose a spinlock over a mutex, and what goes wrong if you spin in user space?
How is a semaphore different from a mutex?

hints.1: Compare what a blocked waiter does: sleep or spin.
hints.2: Weigh acquire latency vs CPU waste, then ownership vs signalling.
hints.3: Spin for CS shorter than a context switch or in interrupt context; mutex otherwise. Semaphore: any process may signal; mutex: only owner unlocks.

phases.goal: Apply synchronization to bounded buffer, readers–writers, dining philosophers, and common coding-level concurrency traps.

must_hit.point: In the naive bounded buffer, count++ and count-- are each load/incr-or-decr/store; interleaved updates can leave count at 2 or 4 instead of 3 when both load count as 3 — that update is a critical section.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows lost update on count and says producer/consumer count updates need mutual exclusion.

must_hit.point: Correct semaphore PC uses empty=n, full=0, binary S=1; down(empty)/down(full) must precede down(S). Taking S first then blocking on full/empty holds the mutex while asleep — classic deadlock.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate orders counting downs before the mutex and explains the deadlock if mutex is taken first.

must_hit.point: Readers–writers: read–read is fine; read–write, write–read, write–write conflict. First reader down(db), last reader up(db); the readers-preference version can starve writers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the conflict table, first/last reader protocol, and writer starvation under continuous readers.

must_hit.point: Dining philosophers: five philosophers and five forks as semaphores; if all take left first, circular wait deadlocks. Fixes: at most four at the table, asymmetric left/right order, or pick up both only if both free under a mutex.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the all-left deadlock and at least one of the three standard fixes.

must_hit.point: Condition-variable wait must use while (!predicate), not if — spurious wakeups or another thread consuming the condition; wait atomically releases and re-acquires the mutex.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate insists on the while loop and mentions spurious wakeup / lost-wakeup closure.

probes: Show how the bounded-buffer count update races, and how semaphores fix it without deadlock.
Why can the dining philosophers deadlock, and how do you prevent it?

hints.1: Focus on one shared index or counter and who can sleep holding a lock.
hints.2: Walk count RMW race → empty/full/S ordering → philosophers' circular wait.
hints.3: Lost count update needs a CS; down counting before mutex; all-left fork grab deadlocks — limit to four, asymmetric order, or both-free under mutex.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Mutex puts waiters to sleep (saves CPU, ~microsecond+ wakeup cost); spinlock busy-waits (near-zero acquire latency, burns cycles). Spin only for CS shorter than a context switch (few microseconds) or contexts that cannot sleep; otherwise mutex. User-space spinning is dangerous if the holder is preempted.

Semaphore is signalling with no owner — any process may up it. Mutex is an owned lock — only the locker unlocks. Binary semaphore can serve as a mutex; a mutex cannot provide semaphore-style cross-process signalling.
Simple LOCK/TAS loops busy-wait; semaphores put blocked processes on a suspended list and sleep, avoiding spinning until up/wakeup.
First/last-reader locking of db allows concurrent readers but a continuous reader stream can starve writers; fair variants prioritize waiting writers.

gotchas.trap: Treating counter, printer-spooler, and buffer bugs as different problems.
gotchas.correction: They share the same defect: an unprotected read–modify–write on a shared index/counter.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a shared LOCK variable provides mutual exclusion.
gotchas.correction: Test and set are non-atomic; two processes can both see LOCK free and both enter.

gotchas.trap: Using strict turn alternation as a complete CS solution.
gotchas.correction: It gives ME but violates progress — a process is blocked by one that may not want to enter.

gotchas.trap: Taking the buffer mutex S before down(empty)/down(full).
gotchas.correction: The process can sleep holding S, so the peer that could wake it never gets S — deadlock. Always down counting semaphores first.
Any process may up a semaphore; only the owner may unlock a mutex.

gotchas.trap: Readers–writers protocol that never considers writers under continuous readers.
gotchas.correction: Readers-preference keeps db locked forever for a stream of readers, starving writers.

gotchas.trap: All dining philosophers take the left fork first.
gotchas.correction: Circular wait deadlock; fix with at most four philosophers, asymmetric fork order, or acquire both only if both free.

gotchas.trap: Waiting on a condition variable with if (!predicate) instead of while.
gotchas.correction: Spurious wakeups or another thread may invalidate the condition; always re-check in a while loop.

gotchas.trap: Relying on volatile for cross-thread correctness in C/C++.
gotchas.correction: volatile stops compiler caching but gives no atomicity or cross-thread ordering — use std::atomic / proper barriers.
CAS checks value not history; fix with version tags, LL/SC, or deferred reclamation (hazard pointers).

gotchas.trap: False sharing of independent per-thread variables.
gotchas.correction: Variables on the same 64-byte cache line bounce between cores; pad/align hot data to its own line.
Enforce a global lock ordering so locks are always acquired in the same fixed order.
